title: Calibration profiles, client throttling, and seedless warmup playbook
content:
Purpose:
This note captures a compact, runnable playbook for throughput calibration runs aimed at repeatable, low-variance benchmarking of the serving runtime. We focus on: how to tune client-side pacing/throttling, a lightweight (seedless) warmup that avoids brittle primer artifacts, and an experiment matrix for statistical repeatability and root-cause profiling. The goal is not to replace the canonical benchmark harness, but to provide a pragmatic, reproducible workflow teams can use for cross-model and cross-hardware comparisons.

Scope and constraints:
- Targeted at single-model pools and multi-model fan-out scenarios where steady-state throughput is the primary metric. Not a latency SLO tuning doc (but we include latency checks).
- Typical hardware: A100/RTX/T4 clusters with Kubernetes orchestration.
- Assumes access to token-level observability (token rates, kv-cache hit-rate) and system metrics (GPU util, PCIe/CPU, memory pressure).

Why this playbook?
Benchmarks drift for many reasons: client burst patterns, RNG/seed differences, cold caches (KV + CUDA kernels), and subtle priming that changes model behavior. The playbook emphasizes: (1) deterministic client pacing with configurable jitter, (2) an approach we call "seedless warmup" that warms internal caches without injecting meaningful semantic prompts, and (3) a small statistical protocol to validate run repeatability.

Key concepts (brief):
- Seedless warmup: execute structurally-valid requests that are intentionally semantically empty (e.g., repeated short padding tokens or mask-only sequences) so we warm inference internals (kernel paths, KV cache allocations) while avoiding model state drift caused by meaningful prefixes.
- Client-side throttling / pacing profiles: define pacing at the request level rather than relying on concurrency limits alone (constant QPS, poisson, burst-with-backoff).
- Calibration profile: a named tuple of (QPS, prompt length distribution, concurrency, arrival pattern, warmup recipe). Keep profiles versioned in the harness repo.

Suggested calibration profiles (examples):
- profile: small-chat-rt
  - target_qps: 120
  - arrival: poisson(lambda=120)
  - prompt-distro: 50% 16-token, 30% 64-token, 20% 128-token
  - concurrency-cap: 30
  - warmup: seedless_2m (see warmup recipes)

- profile: long-context-batch
  - target_qps: 18
  - arrival: constant-rate
  - prompt-distro: 100% 1024-token
  - concurrency-cap: 8
  - warmup: seedless_5m

Client loadgen config knobs (practical):
- connections_per_client: 4 (keep >1 so TLS handshakes amortize)
- request_timeout: generous (60s) during warmup, stricter (15s) in measurement window
- pacing_mode: [constant-qps | poisson | staircase]
- jitter_pct: 4–8% on top of pacing to avoid micro-synchrony
- tokenization_mode: offline-tokenize to ensure stable token counts across clients
- retry_policy: DO NOT retry within measurement window; record failures and surface them in run report

Seedless warmup recipes (practical sequences):
- seedless_2m (fast): 2 minutes per replica
  - pattern: repeated NOP prompt arrays (e.g., `[[PAD]]` * 8 tokens) with generation length 8
  - rate: 0.75 * target_qps to avoid saturating thermal limits
  - purpose: warm model kernels, kv allocator, and initial CUDA kernels
- seedless_5m (robust): 5 minutes per replica
  - phase 1 (2m): short NOP prompts at 0.6 * QPS
  - phase 2 (2m): mid-length synthetic prompts (64 tokens) at 0.4 * QPS to exercise attention mechanisms
  - phase 3 (1m): single-shot target QPS spike for kernel priming

Why seedless vs priming with real prompts:
Priming with meaningful prompts reduces variance for downstream language outputs but introduces data-dependent state (token distributions in KV caches) and can make runs hard to compare across models. Seedless warmup minimizes semantic leakage and focuses on warming system internals. For regressions that affect output quality we still run separate real-prompt evaluations (Evals pipeline).

Repeatability checks and statistical protocol:
- Minimum runs: 5 independent measurement runs per profile. Independent means restart harness client processes and clear client RNG seeds.
- Measurement window: 10 minutes steady-state after warmup (longer for long-context workloads).
- Metrics to capture per-run: P50/P95/P99 latency, mean throughput (tokens/sec and requests/sec), GPU util by percentile, tail queue depth, error rate, token-generation-efficiency (tokens/sec per GPU), kv-cache-hit-rate.
- Stability criteria: across 5 runs, mean throughput coefficient of variation (CoV) should be < 3% for acceptance. If CoV between 3–7% mark as flaky and investigate. >7%: fail and root-cause.
- Drift detection: compute run-to-run KL divergence on request-length distribution and tokenization counts; if KL > 0.08 investigate client-side tokenization mismatch.

Profiling & instrumentation checklist:
- Enable GPU perf metrics (nvml/nvidia-smi sampling at 1s granularity)
- Capture system-level counters: CPU steal, IO wait, network rx/tx, and NIC queue depths
- Record runtime traces: per-request spans (ingest, tokenize, ams, attention, decode) and overall KV cache hit/miss counts if available
- Collect kernel timestamps for large-attention kernels and matrix ops (if kernel-level telemetry is available via runtime)
- Log GPU driver re-compilations and first-call kernel latencies separately (should be zero after warmup)

Runbook (step-by-step):
1) Ensure cluster is in test quiescent state (no other noisy jobs).
2) Deploy model revision on a dedicated pool with monitoring enabled and model pinned.
3) Start client harness with seedless warmup profile (clients restarted to reset RNG).
4) Wait for warmup to complete. Validate: no driver recompile logs in monitor, GPU util stable for 30s.
5) Start measurement window. Do not change pacing or concurrency mid-window.
6) Stop harness and collect artifacts: loadgen logs, perf metrics, traces, and system snapshots.
7) Repeat steps 3–6 N=5 runs.
8) Aggregate metrics and run repeatability checks.

Common failure modes and quick mitigations:
- High variance on run N: suspect background noise — re-run with cluster-iso snapshot or use dedicated nodes.
- Frequent transport errors: check keepalive / TLS connections per client, reduce connections_per_client or increase connection pool.
- Warmup still showing kernel recompiles: extend seedless warmup by +2 minutes and add a final high-rate spike.
- Latency tail spikes correlated with CPU steal: migrate clients to dedicated control-plane nodes with less host load.

Artifacts to upload with each benchmark run (mandatory):
- loadgen raw logs (compressed)
- harness config file (JSON/YAML) with profile version tag
- aggregated run metrics CSV
- perf snapshots (GPU, system)
- span traces (if available)
- short run summary (1-paragraph) describing anomalies

Notes and gotchas:
- Avoid mixing real prompt warmups and measurement runs in the same job unless explicitly testing semantic cache effects.
- Tokenization must be stable and deterministic across clients; prefer centralized tokenization step in the harness.
- When comparing models with different tokenizer vocab sizes, normalize by tokens-per-request in the report.

Next steps / action items:
- Add these calibration profiles into loadbench repo as named YAMLs (see linked PR).
- Automate the repeatability CoV report and add CI gating for model-serving PRs.
- Expand seedless recipes to include batch size sweeps for GPU kernel coverage.

Contacts for help: Marcus Li (bench harness lead), Eleni Georgiou (runtime profiling), Infra SRE channel (#infra-sre).

Appendix: short example client config (YAML snippet)
---
client_name: calibrator-01
connections_per_client: 4
pacing_mode: poisson
poisson_lambda: 120
jitter_pct: 6
seedless_warmup: seedless_5m
measurement_window_seconds: 600
retry_policy: none
log_level: info
---

End of playbook. Keep this doc as a working checklist — please annotate with run ids and observations below when you execute a run.
